title: How do we do family devotions?
seoTitle: How to Do Family Devotions, From Toddlers to Teens
description: Five minutes at the table or bedtime counts. Family devotions for little ones, school-age kids, and teens, and how to start again when it falls apart.
summary: Five minutes at the table or bedtime: a few verses, a question, a prayer. Faith at home, by age, without the guilt.
askedAs: how to teach kids the Bible
answer: You want your children to know God at home, not only at church, and when you try, it falls apart. The three-year-old won't sit, the eight-year-old is poking his sister, the teenager stares at the ceiling, and you wonder if you're doing more harm than good. Or nobody ever did this with you, and you can't picture it. Start smaller than you think. Pick one meal or one bedtime, read a few verses aloud, ask one question, and pray, even a single sentence. Five minutes counts. Little ones need a story, a song, and a one-line prayer. School-age children can take a passage, a question, and a prayer each child says. Teenagers need you to ask what they're wondering and then talk less. When a night goes badly, try again tomorrow.
happening:
If you're reading this, you may have already tried. You gathered everyone after dinner and opened the Bible, and inside two minutes the youngest was on the floor, someone was laughing at the wrong thing, and you were reading about the love of God through clenched teeth.

Every stage has its own version. Parents of little ones are so tired that five more minutes feels like a mountain. School-age children come with practices, homework, and a calendar that eats the evening. With teenagers it can feel too late, as if the door closed while you weren't looking. Some of you are doing this alone, or in a blended family where the children split the week between two houses, or beside a spouse who doesn't believe. Others came to faith as adults and have no memory of a praying home to copy. And if devotions in your childhood were used as a weapon, a lecture after a fight or a verse aimed at a sin, you may have promised yourself you'd never do that to your own children, and then done nothing, which doesn't feel right either.

The usual explanations each hold some truth. One says you need more discipline, and habits do matter; a practice tied to a time you already keep will outlast good intentions. Another says this is what church is for, and children do need a whole church and not only a family, but an hour on Sunday can't do what a home does on a Tuesday night. The skeptic adds a third: that teaching children religion presses on minds too young to push back. Some of you felt that pressure as children, and the objection gets a fair answer below.

What these leave out is the picture in our heads. Many of us imagine family devotions as a small church service in the living room, with a lesson, a lecture, and a quiet test of whether everyone got the point, kept faithfully every night by some other family who seems to manage it. That picture makes the whole thing feel forced and makes one bad night feel like failure. Scripture's picture is plainer and kinder: God's words spoken in the ordinary hours a family already has (Deuteronomy 6:7). A few verses, a question, and a prayer at the table or on the edge of a bed belong in that picture, and so does the night it falls apart halfway through and you pray anyway.

scripture.intro: Scripture doesn't hand families a devotional format, and it doesn't pretend faithful homes are calm. These passages put faith in the ordinary day, welcome children, read a famous household verse in its setting, and trace one young man's faith to his grandmother and mother.

passages.text: And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength. These words I am commanding you today are to be upon your hearts. And you shall teach them diligently to your children and speak of them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up.
passages.reading: Deuteronomy presents these words as Moses' charge to Israel before they entered the land, with “your children and grandchildren” already in view (Deuteronomy 6:2). The teaching starts with the parent's own love for God and with these words on the parent's own heart. Then it reaches the children in the course of a day: at home, on the road, at bedtime, first thing in the morning. A little later Deuteronomy expects a child to ask what all these commands mean, and the answer begins with a story: “We were slaves of Pharaoh in Egypt, but the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand” (Deuteronomy 6:21), and only then comes round to the commands. The child's question is expected, and the first thing it gets is what God has done.

passages.text: Now people were bringing the little children to Jesus for Him to place His hands on them, and the disciples rebuked those who brought them. But when Jesus saw this, He was indignant and told them, “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these. Truly I tell you, anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.” And He took the children in His arms, placed His hands on them, and blessed them.
passages.reading: The disciples rebuked the people who brought little children, as if children were an interruption to the real work, and Mark says Jesus was indignant. He made a little child the picture of how anyone receives the kingdom of God (Mark 10:15), then took the children in his arms and spoke a blessing over them. The three-year-old who can't sit still is part of the real thing, and may be better at receiving than you are. A family's worship with no room for wiggling, interruptions, or odd questions has room for fewer people than Jesus did.

passages.text: But if it is unpleasing in your sight to serve the LORD, then choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve, whether the gods your fathers served beyond the Euphrates, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you are living. As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD!”
passages.reading: This is the verse on doormats and kitchen plaques. Joshua, now old, gathers the tribes of Israel at Shechem (Joshua 23:1; 24:1). Before he asks for anything, he retells what God had done, beginning with ancestors beyond the Euphrates who “worshiped other gods” and ending in the land they now live in (Joshua 24:2-13). Then he sets a real choice before them, declares his own, and leaves theirs to them. When the people promise to serve the LORD, he answers, “You are not able to serve the LORD, for He is a holy God” (Joshua 24:19). The sequel is sobering. After Joshua's generation died, “another generation rose up who did not know the LORD or the works that He had done for Israel” (Judges 2:10). Judges doesn't stop to say why. A sign by the door is a good thing, but it can't do the telling.

passages.text: But as for you, continue in the things you have learned and firmly believed, since you know from whom you have learned them. From infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.
passages.reading: The second letter to Timothy, a letter in Paul's name, presents itself as a farewell (2 Timothy 4:6). It reminds Timothy that he has known the Scriptures from infancy and knows whom he learned from, and it has already said where his faith began: “your sincere faith, which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice” (2 Timothy 1:5). Acts calls his mother a Jewish believer and says only that his father was a Greek (Acts 16:1). If you're the only believer in your house, a single parent, or a grandparent with a child on your lap, you're standing close to where Lois and Eunice stood. And the passage names the aim, which is larger than good behavior: wisdom for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.

whyHard:
The usual explanation is that we're too busy, and there's truth in it, but tired parents are nothing new. Busyness explains why it's hard to start; it can't explain why it feels so strange once we do.

Part of the strangeness is that we've forgotten how old this is. Deuteronomy gave all Israel the charge to teach their children at home and on the road, and observant Jews still say the Shema, which begins with Deuteronomy 6:4, every morning and evening, taking “when you lie down and when you get up” at its word (Deuteronomy 6:7). And when Martin Luther found that ordinary people in the village parishes of Saxony knew almost nothing of the faith, he wrote a small catechism, published in 1529, and framed each part for the head of a household to teach simply at home.

Then came a mercy. In 1780 Robert Raikes started a Sunday school in Gloucester, England, for poor children who often worked the other six days, and they learned to read from the Bible. Sunday schools spread, and many of us grew up in churches where volunteers taught the Bible to children down the hall, which is a gift too. But a gift can become a substitute without anyone deciding it should, and this one easily does. We absorb a lesson nobody meant to teach: faith is a subject, and subjects belong to specialists. So when we try at home, we copy the specialists, and the little church service in the living room is the result. It feels forced because it's borrowed.

Beneath that sits a second assumption: that devotions are a technique, and a technique should work. We read Proverbs 22:6 as a contract. If the children stay in the faith, the method worked; if they wander, we failed. That turns a family's prayer into a performance, with the children as the audience and their future as the grade. An anxious parent pushing for a result comes close to what Scripture warns against: the sentence in the letter to the Ephesians that tells fathers to bring children up “in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” first says, “do not provoke your children to wrath” (Ephesians 6:4).

Others of us hold back for the opposite reason: we grew up with faith forced on us, or we've heard that teaching a child religion is indoctrination. The worry is fair, since a parent can use a child's trust to shut down questions the child should be free to ask. But there's no neutral home, and the real line runs between teaching that welcomes questions and teaching that forbids them. Scripture, which keeps picturing a child who asks (Exodus 12:26; Joshua 4:6), stands with the question.

I'm a pastor and the father of five sons, and I'm inside this. We pastors have built children's programs and let parents assume the work was handled, and we've preached family worship in ways that left tired parents feeling like failures. Between the two, faith at home can start to look like a program to run and a result to secure, when Scripture pictures a family speaking of God out loud, day after day, telling the truth about him and about themselves. Jesus told Nicodemus that being born of the Spirit is like the wind: “The wind blows where it wishes” (John 3:8). We can't give our children faith. We can make sure they never have to guess what we loved.

thisWeek.intro: You don't need a curriculum, only five minutes you can keep. Start with the first step, take whichever of the next three fits your children's ages, add a song when you're ready, and save the last step for the night it all falls apart.

steps.title: Pick a time, then read, ask, and pray
steps.body: Attach this to something that already happens most days: the end of dinner, breakfast if mornings are calm, or bedtime with little ones. Read a few verses aloud, such as a story from Genesis, a scene from Mark, or a psalm. Ask one question you don't know the answer to, like *What do you notice about Jesus here?*, and let the answers be odd. Pray for real things by name, and stop while it's going well. If you can't share a meal most days, choose one a week and protect it. On a night with more time, the [Family Devotion Builder](/tools/family-devotions) makes a fifteen-minute devotion for your children's ages.

steps.title: For little ones: a story, a song, a one-line prayer
steps.body: Toddlers and preschoolers can't sit still for long, and they don't have to. Tell one short Bible story and let them act it out or hold something while you read. Sing one simple song. Teach a prayer they can say with you, such as *Thank you, God, for today.* At bedtime, put your hand on their head and speak the words God gave Israel's priests: “May the LORD bless you and keep you” (Numbers 6:24). Two minutes is plenty.

steps.title: For school-age children: a passage, a question, everyone prays
steps.body: Children of about six to eleven can follow a real passage and argue about it. Let a child who likes to read do the reading. Ask your question, then wait longer than feels comfortable before answering it yourself. End with a prayer each child says in a sentence of their own. It's a good age to add one question a week from the [Family Catechism](/family/catechism).

steps.title: For teenagers: their questions first
steps.body: Start with what they're wondering. Ask what they find hard to believe, or what their friends say about Christians, and hear the whole answer. Talk less than they do, let them choose the passage or lead now and then, and give them full permission to disagree out loud. If the family time has gone stale, try one-on-one, in the car or over a late snack. And don't use the time to settle last night's argument.

steps.title: Add a song, and follow the seasons
steps.body: Sing something together: a hymn, a psalm set to music, a song from church. Then let the church year give you a rhythm. Many churches keep Advent, the four Sundays before Christmas, and Holy Week, from Palm Sunday to Easter, and those stories belong in any home. The [Family Devotions](/family/devotions) page has a booklet for each to print, a reading a day, and [How to Keep Advent as a Family](/how-tos/fam-how-to-keep-advent-as-a-family) adds candles and a wreath.

steps.title: When it falls apart, start again
steps.body: It will. Someone gets sick, a game runs late, a custody weekend breaks the rhythm, or you simply forget for two weeks. Don't make a speech about it, and don't wait for Monday. Open the Bible at the next meal as if nothing happened. In a hard season, shrink it rather than drop it: one verse and a one-line prayer in the car counts. Nobody keeps this without missing. Keeping it means starting again.

moreHelp.body:
Much of what makes family devotions hard belongs with patience, a friend who has been there, and your pastor. But when you make room for questions, children sometimes bring out something heavier than a question, and the signs below tell you when to call someone right away. Some homes also carry harm that no devotional can fix. If someone in your home uses Scripture or prayer to frighten, threaten, or control, that's spiritual abuse. If that's happening, or you're afraid of your spouse, your safety and your children's come first: call 911 if anyone is in danger right now, and the National Domestic Violence Hotline, with the other help lines at the end of this page, can help you plan. With a partner you fear, couples counseling isn't the place to start; talk with an advocate or a counselor on your own first.

For a child's fears that won't settle, start with your child's doctor, who can refer you on. A licensed counselor can help with those fears, with a marriage where faith has become a constant fight, and with old religious wounds that reopen when you lead your own family; look for a professional counselor, a marriage and family therapist, a clinical social worker, or a psychologist. Ask your doctor for names, check your insurer's directory, or ask a pastor which counselors they trust, and confirm the license with your state's licensing board. If you want a Christian counselor, ask about training and license as well as faith.
signs: A child talks about wanting to die or hurting themselves. Call or text 988 now, or 911 if they're in danger.
A child tells you someone is hurting them. Believe them, keep them safe, and call 911 if they're in danger now, or else the police or your state's child abuse hotline.
A child's fear of God, hell, or doing wrong keeps them from sleeping for weeks, and no reassurance settles it.
Someone at home uses Scripture or prayer to frighten, threaten, or control, or you're afraid of your spouse.
Leading devotions brings back fear or shame from how faith was forced on you, and it doesn't ease.
You share custody and disagree about your children's religious upbringing. Talk to a family lawyer before you act.
moreHelp.firstCall: You can keep it simple: *My nine-year-old has become afraid of God. She asks every night whether she's going to hell, and nothing I say helps for long.* Or: *My spouse and I can't talk about church and the kids without fighting.* If you're afraid of your spouse, say that first and ask to be seen on your own. Ask whether the counselor is licensed in your state, whether they work with children or families, how they handle a family's faith, and what it costs. With a lawyer, ask what your custody order says.
moreHelp.cost: A visit to your child's doctor is often covered by insurance. Counseling costs vary, so ask before you begin, and ask about sliding-scale fees. Community mental health centers, university training clinics, and employee assistance programs offer lower-cost care, and your church may have a benevolence fund. For a custody question, legal aid or a bar association's lawyer referral service can point you to affordable help. The devotions, catechism, and booklets on this site are free.

helping.body:
If you're a grandparent, you may be the Lois in a child's life (2 Timothy 1:5). Ask the parents before you start anything with their children, especially if they don't share your faith, and honor their answer. Tell your grandchildren what God has done in your life, and pray with them when you're invited.

If you're a pastor or you lead families at church, equip parents rather than shaming them. Teach the five-minute shape, and send families home on Sunday with one question for the table. Remember the single parent, the parent whose spouse doesn't believe, and the parent who never saw this done. If a parent tells you they're afraid of their spouse, or that Scripture is being used against them at home, believe them, ask how it's safe to reach them, and point them to the National Domestic Violence Hotline instead of suggesting the couple sit down together. If you work with children, learn your church's child-safety policy and your state's reporting rules now; many states make clergy mandated reporters, the rules vary, and this isn't legal advice.

If you're a friend, invite a family to dinner and let them see five ordinary minutes of Scripture and prayer at a real table, spills and all.
say: It's okay that it fell apart. Start again tonight.
Come for dinner Sunday? We read a few verses at the end. Nothing fancy.
Tell me about your kids. What can I pray for?
(To a grandchild's parents) May I pray with the kids at bedtime when they stay with us?
dontSay: Our family never misses a night.
If you really cared about their souls, you'd make time.
Do this, and they'll never leave the faith.
Just make them sit still and listen.
helping.next: Offer something concrete: print the Advent or Holy Week booklet for a family before the season starts, or send them the Family Devotion Builder with a note. Check back in a few weeks without making it a quiz, and pray for their children by name. Pastors, keep a short list of licensed family counselors you trust, for the day a question at someone's table turns out heavier than it looked.

prayer:
Lord, you gave us these children, and most nights we don't know what we're doing. We want them to know you. We're tired, and we're afraid we started too late, or did it wrong, or taught them more with our tempers than with our prayers.

Be at our table. When the milk spills and the little ones won't sit, let them still hear your name spoken with love. When our teenagers push back, keep us from lecturing and give us patience to listen. Where our own faith is thin, let them hear us ask you for help instead of pretending.

We can't make them believe. Only you give faith. So we put them in your hands, and we'll keep telling them what you've done, as well as we can, for as long as you give us.

Jesus, you took the children in your arms. Take ours. Amen.

faq.q: How do you do family devotions with teenagers?
faq.a: Change the form and keep the faith at the center. Start with their questions instead of your lesson, such as what they find hard to believe, then talk less than they do and let them disagree out loud; an argument means they're still talking to you. Faithful parents differ on whether to require an older teenager to be there. Some require it, as they'd require a seat at dinner, because while a child lives at home the family's worship is part of the family's life, and Joshua answered for his whole house (Joshua 24:15). Others invite without requiring, because faith can't be compelled and a near-adult pressed into worship can come to resent it, and the letter to the Ephesians tells fathers not to provoke their children (Ephesians 6:4). Both can be done in love, and neither one decides your child's faith; just never make it a punishment, and never make your love depend on their agreement. If your teenager says they don't believe anymore, read [When Your Teenager Says They Don't Believe Anymore](/writing/teenager-losing-faith).

faq.q: My spouse isn't a Christian. Can I still do devotions with our kids?
faq.a: Yes, and do it in the open. Your spouse is your children's parent too, and faith that is forced or hidden teaches children that God is what divides their parents. Talk first, and look for what you can agree on: bedtime prayers with you, Bible stories, the children coming with you to church. Invite, never force, and never use devotions to criticize the other parent. Let your children see your faith in how you treat the one who doesn't share it. Timothy's faith first lived in his grandmother and his mother, and Acts says only that his father was a Greek (2 Timothy 1:5; Acts 16:1). If you're afraid of your spouse, safety comes first; the help lines are at the end of this page.

faq.q: I'm a single parent. How do I do family devotions on my own?
faq.a: The same way, only smaller, and with help. Choose the easiest anchor you have, often bedtime or the drive to school, and keep it to a few minutes; God knows how much you're carrying. If your children live in two homes, keep the practice on your days without criticizing the other house. Then widen the circle: ask a grandparent, a friend, or a family at church to pray with your children or have them to dinner now and then, so they know more than one adult who loves God. Timothy's faith first lived in his grandmother and his mother (2 Timothy 1:5), and Scripture names those two women only once, for the faith they handed on.

faq.q: What is a catechism, and should we use one with our kids?
faq.a: A catechism is a set of questions and answers about the faith, learned by heart and said aloud, such as *Who made you?* answered with *God made me.* Christians have taught this way for centuries, and words learned early are there to reach for later. Pick one, ideally one your church uses, and take one question a week at a meal: you ask, everyone answers together, and you add a sentence of explanation. The site's [Family Catechism](/family/catechism) has seventy-six questions, each with an answer for adults, a shorter one for children, and a verse from the Berean Standard Bible.

faq.q: Isn't teaching kids religion just indoctrination?
faq.a: It can be, and the objection deserves a fair hearing. Children trust their parents, and a parent can use that trust to close questions a child should be free to ask, or to frighten a child into agreement. That does real harm. But no home is neutral; a family teaches what matters by how it spends its evenings, its money, and its anger, and silence about God teaches children something too. The difference is how you teach: whether questions are welcome, the hard parts are told honestly, and a child can disagree without losing your love. I came to faith from atheism, so I take this objection seriously, and I'd rather a child examine this faith than inherit it unexamined.

faq.q: Does Proverbs 22:6 promise my kids will stay in the faith?
faq.a: No. “Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it” (Proverbs 22:6) is a proverb, a saying about how life usually runs in God's world, not a contract. What a child learns young tends to last, and that's real encouragement. But Scripture doesn't pretend it always does. Of the prophet Samuel it says, “his sons did not walk in his ways” (1 Samuel 8:3), and through Isaiah God says of his own people, “I have raised children and brought them up, but they have rebelled against Me” (Isaiah 1:2). If a child you raised in the faith has walked away, the proverb isn't a verdict on you. Every parent fails in ways worth confessing, but a child's faith was never yours to secure. Family devotions are your family's worship, offered because God is worthy, and only God gives faith.

faq.q: Can I lead family devotions if I'm not sure what I believe?
faq.a: Yes, if you're honest. You don't have to perform a certainty you don't have. Read the stories, ask the questions, and when a child asks something you can't answer, say *I don't know; let's find out together.* You can pray as a desperate father did when he brought his son to Jesus: “I do believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24). But carry your heaviest doubts to another adult, not to your children. [I'm not sure I believe anymore](/help/doubt) and [How to Answer Your Child's Hard Questions About God](/how-tos/parenting-how-to-answer-hard-questions-about-god) are good places to start.

slots.note: For the reader who never saw a praying home: if James wants, a few sentences in his own words on what it was like to begin praying and reading Scripture with his own family, and whether he had any example to copy (he was raised without a father and came to faith from atheism; nothing more about his childhood is assumed). Only from James. The page names his coming to faith from atheism once, in the answer on indoctrination, never mentions his growing up without a father, and stands without this.

The last paragraph implicates pastors as 'we' (children's programs that let parents assume the work was handled, and preaching that left tired parents feeling like failures) and claims nothing about James's own church or home. If he wants to make that self-implication personal, only in his own words.

What family devotions actually look like in James's home with five sons (the time of day, what they read, what fell apart and how they started again), if he is willing to share it. Only from James; no invented scenes with his sons.

Where James lands on requiring an older teenager to be present for family devotions, in his own words. The teenager answer states both views in their own terms (require it, as part of the family's life, with Joshua 24:15; invite without requiring, since faith can't be compelled, with Ephesians 6:4), gives shared counsel, and deliberately does not land.

Confirm, change, or cut the conviction written for James at the end of the indoctrination answer: 'I came to faith from atheism, so I take this objection seriously, and I'd rather a child examine this faith than inherit it unexamined.' It is offered as a conviction, not a story, and ties his stance only to the bare fact of his coming to faith from atheism; it should stay only if he would say it himself.

Whether James uses or recommends a particular catechism for families, and why. The catechism answer points to the site's Family Catechism and to one the reader's own church uses, and names no tradition for him.

Any family or child counselors near Fenton that James trusts enough to name, and whether First Baptist Church of Fenton has a child-safety and reporting policy for its children's and youth leaders. Only from James.
